analysis.one_liner: Establishes a universal government health program covering every U.S. resident, including long-term care, prescription drugs, and free preventive care.
analysis.headline: The universal health care bill died in committee: after referral to three House committees and three subcommittees, it never received a hearing, a vote, or action from the full House before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have guaranteed health coverage to every U.S. citizen and permanent resident, either through a new public 'USHealth Program' (built by expanding Medicare) or through certified employer health plans. It would add prescription drug coverage, end coinsurance for inpatient hospital care, cap yearly out-of-pocket costs at $1,500 per person, and create a universal long-term care benefit covering home care and nursing home care regardless of age. Employers would be required to enroll their workers in a certified plan or the public program, and the financing would come from payroll premiums, removing the cap on wages subject to Medicare taxes, and raising the health insurance tax rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone without health insurance would gain guaranteed coverage, including long-term care that Medicare and most private plans do not cover. Seniors would get prescription drug, dental, vision, and hearing benefits with no deductibles or co-pays on preventive care. Anyone facing a hospital stay would no longer owe coinsurance, and no family could be billed past a $2,000 annual cap. Low-income people could get help paying premiums and co-pays, and workers could no longer be denied or priced out of employer plans because of pre-existing conditions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured Americans, seniors, and families needing long-term care

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes every U.S. citizen and permanent resident eligible for hospital and medical benefits under a new USHealth Program, unless they are enrolled in a qualified employer plan, effectively guaranteeing universal coverage.

It adds prescription drugs, preventive services (prenatal care, well-child care, mammograms, pap smears, colorectal screening, family planning, and risk-factor counseling) to Medicare coverage, and prohibits the Board from using a formulary to exclude any covered drug.

It creates a long-term care benefit for all residents regardless of age or disability, covering home and community-based services, respite care, and nursing facility care with unlimited duration as long as need continues.
It eliminates coinsurance for inpatient hospital stays and caps annual out-of-pocket cost-sharing at $1,500 per individual and $2,000 per family, with providers barred from billing past the cap.

It requires employers to enroll all full-time, part-time, seasonal, and temporary employees in a qualified health plan or the public program, bars health-status discrimination and pre-existing condition exclusions, and requires community-rated premiums that cannot vary by age or gender.
It adds low-income assistance to limit or eliminate premiums, deductibles, and co-payments for low-income enrollees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would owe enrollment or payment obligations for every employee, including part-time and temporary workers. High earners would pay substantially more in payroll taxes, since the bill removes the wage cap on Medicare taxes and raises the health insurance tax rate. Hospitals, doctors, drug makers, and insurers would face capped payment rates, an annual overall spending limit negotiated by provider class, and community-rated insurance rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, high earners, and health care providers

drawbacks.text: Financing falls on employers and high-income earners: the bill removes the cap on wages subject to Medicare taxes and increases the health insurance tax rate, while employers must pay to enroll part-time and temporary workers they currently may not cover.

Cost control relies on an overall annual spending cap for the program, with the Board negotiating payment allocations among provider classes each year — a mechanism that could squeeze hospital and physician payments or constrain access to services.

The bill eliminates all mandatory Medicaid benefits in favor of the new program and repeals COBRA continuation coverage, replacing existing programs with a phased-in system that could leave gaps during the transition.

The long-term care benefit requires a Screening Agency and a Case Management Agency in every area to determine eligibility and manage care — a large new bureaucracy whose quality and cost were untested.

Coverage of employed people would still flow through private employer plans rather than the public program, keeping workers dependent on a certified but still-private insurance market with premium limits and mandates that employers could resist as a cost.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains are large: universal coverage, a first-of-its-kind universal long-term care benefit, drug coverage, and a hard cap on out-of-pocket medical costs. The honest costs are equally large — new payroll taxes falling on employers and high earners, capped provider payments that hospitals and physicians would fight, and an annual global spending limit that critics could fairly call rationing by budget rather than by medical judgment. The hybrid design (public program for non-workers, mandated private plans for workers) added administrative complexity compared with a single-payer bill, and phasing out Medicaid's mandatory benefits created real transition risk for low-income patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then three subcommittees, and none of them ever reported it, held a vote, or moved it to the floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Roybal of California introduced the USHealth Program Act on October 9, 1991.
The House referred it to three committees with jurisdiction over health programs — Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means.
In October 1991 and March 1992, it was referred to three subcommittees (Health; Health and the Environment; and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness; and Labor-Management Relations).
No further action appears in the record: no hearings on the bill itself, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote. The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
The bill had 12 cosponsors, 11 Democrats and 1 Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, drug makers, hospitals, and employers were better off because the bill died — none of them faced a universal public program, an employer coverage mandate, community-rated premiums, or a global cap on health spending. Americans without health insurance and families without long-term care coverage gained nothing; they remained in the same system until later reform proposals in the 1990s.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers, drug makers, and employers

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and 11 of the 12 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican cosponsor; no vote ever occurred, so there is no roll-call record of how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would put a competing public program under everyone not covered by employer insurance and force employment-related plans to accept community-rated premiums, guaranteed renewability, and no health-status discrimination — shrinking the practices insurers used to avoid covering sick people. Insurers would keep the large employer-plan market, but under certification standards and premium limits set by the new USHealth Board.

Medicare would begin paying for outpatient prescription drugs, with payment limits tied to surveyed wholesale prices and a published physician price guide. The bill bars a formulary, but the payment caps and price surveys directly cut into drug pricing power.

Universal coverage would mean far fewer uninsured patients and no patient coinsurance for hospital stays, but the bill imposes an annual overall spending cap and requires the USHealth Board to adjust payment rates by provider class each year. Doctors with financial ties to home IV therapy providers would face referral bans and civil money penalties.

industries.industry: Home care and nursing home providers
industries.note: A universal long-term care benefit would create a permanent public payer for home care, respite, and nursing facility services for everyone regardless of age, with case-management agencies maintaining registries of qualified providers. Providers would gain a huge new payer, though with certification and quality-assurance requirements.

industries.industry: Employers (especially those with part-time and temporary workforces)
industries.note: Every employer would have to enroll full-time, part-time, seasonal, and temporary workers in a certified plan or the public program, and nonenrolling employers would owe payments to the fund. Employees currently off the insurance rolls — part-timers, seasonal and temp workers — would gain coverage at the employer's expense.

The bill gives 'favorable treatment of network plans and utilization review programs' and requires HMOs to provide outpatient mental health services, building managed care into the new system rather than displacing it. HMOs would operate inside the new framework with guaranteed customers, but with quality-assurance and consumer-protection obligations.
